done.why: I spent my last eighty-odd turns wandering a maze of twisty little passages that all look alike. Once I found the grating room I overshot it and could never find it again. The maze rooms give the reader nothing at all: one line and no exits listed. My patience ran out before the maze did.

about: It's the old white house and the great underground beneath it: a field, a mailbox, a trophy case waiting to be filled, then a troll, a thief, a bat, a maze, a hoard of treasures. The map and the puzzles are mostly the old ones. What has changed is the voice. When you look closely at things, the prose is wry and a little melancholy. It is full of dead adventurers and things left behind, and about how the dark wins in the end ("Its batteries gave out some time before its owner did, which, down here, is the usual order of things"). It's about taking treasure, and about the people who tried before you and didn't make it home.

moments.note: The trophy case 'has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.' A piece of furniture with a personality, and it's the first sign that someone wrote these closely.
The sword 'has plainly been in worse places than a living room.' Dry and funny.
The troll description, with teeth 'not all of them his own' and watching me 'the way a cook watches a chicken.' Best line so far.
I kept swinging after the troll had already vanished. That was my own fault, but it cost three turns of 'You can't see any such thing.'
Touching the mirror shook the room and moved me to an identical Mirror Room. After that I couldn't tell which one I was in, and the descriptions are word for word the same.
The crystal trident: 'Light goes into it and comes out somewhere else. It was made for someone who expected to be obeyed by the sea.' Lovely.
The bat carried me off even though I had garlic in the sack. Apparently it has to be in hand. Fair enough, but it stung.
Listening in the Squeaky Room: 'something that sounds remarkably like "Fweep!"' Funny, and it set up the bat.
The thief walked through and took the trident and the bracelet while I was busy fumbling with an object that wasn't there. I lost my two best finds.
The bat, 'a large vampire bat, as bats go, and he goes', has 'come to an understanding with the dark' and is holding his nose with both wings. Wonderful.
The chasm: 'a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.' I reread it.
The chimney refusal names everything I'm carrying and says exactly what fits: 'you, your lamp and one thing more, and not an inch besides.' A clear and fair rule.
The inventory showed the bottle indented under the sack, but the game said it isn't in the sack. 'empty sack' wasn't understood either.
The thief killed me. The death text is new and kind: plain things strewn in the fields, valuables rolled into dark corners, and 'somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.'
I stumbled straight onto the skeleton in the maze. The skeleton, key, lantern and rusty knife all have beautiful, sad descriptions.
I reached the Grating Room, the way out the skull key surely fits, and then my next move took me straight back into the maze. I never found it again.
Dozens of 'Maze' / 'You can't go that way.' The writing that made the rest a joy is completely absent here.

wished: I wished the maze rooms had even one distinguishing detail. Everything else is so richly described that the bare 'Maze' lines felt like a different game.
I wished I could drop things to mark my way, or that the game told me the exits.
I wished 'empty sack' worked, and that the inventory made clear what was inside what.
I wished garlic carried in the sack counted against the bat, or that something hinted it had to be held.
I wished the two Mirror Rooms read differently so I knew which side of the mirror I was on.
I wished I could have fought the thief on fairer terms. He took my best treasures and then my life before I understood he was there.

lines.line: It has the patient air of something that expects to be filled.
lines.why: It made the trophy case a quiet character and gave the whole game its purpose in one sentence.

lines.line: He is watching you the way a cook watches a chicken.
lines.why: Menace and comedy at once. It told me this was written by someone who enjoys sentences.

lines.line: Light goes into it and comes out somewhere else. It was made for someone who expected to be obeyed by the sea.
lines.why: The most beautiful object description I read. It makes the trident feel genuinely precious.

lines.line: It is far too fine for a coal mine, and somebody must once have thought so too, and then had a reason to leave in a hurry.
lines.why: One sentence about a bracelet with a whole story hidden in it.

lines.line: He is a large vampire bat, as bats go, and he goes: leathery, beady-eyed and plainly unwell in his mind.
lines.why: The pun on 'goes' delighted me. Nobody writes a bat like that.

lines.line: Whoever carved it had all the time in the world, and used it.
lines.why: A calm, warm ending to the jade figurine. It made me want to keep it.

lines.line: The chasm drops away from your feet into a dark that your lamp does not so much light as annoy.
lines.why: Perfect phrasing. The follow-up about whoever kicked the last pebble is darkly funny too.

lines.line: anything of value has rolled into some dark corner in or under it, and somebody tidy has put the lamp back in the living room.
lines.why: Being killed was softened by real wit, and the line also told me what had happened to my things.

lines.line: Whatever he came into the maze looking for, the maze found him first.
lines.why: The skeleton's epitaph. It foreshadowed my own long, lost hour in that maze.

lines.line: Its batteries gave out some time before its owner did, which, down here, is the usual order of things.
lines.why: Grim, funny, and a real warning about my own lamp.

lines.line: The rust has not touched the edge. That is not a thing rust usually overlooks.
lines.why: A small uncanny hook. It made me suspicious of a knife.

fun.why: The first hundred turns were a pleasure: the troll fight, the trident, the bat, the chimney rule, and stumbling on the skeleton. The thief stripping me and then killing me hurt. The last eighty turns in the maze were no fun at all.

engagement.why: Examining things kept me reading and rereading, and every examine paid off. Engagement fell off a cliff in the maze, where there was nothing to read and nothing to examine.

difficulty.why: The thief steals and kills with little warning. Garlic has to be held, not bagged. The two mirror rooms are indistinguishable. The maze gives no footholds. I made progress, but often through luck (finding the skeleton by chance) rather than understanding.

interestingness.why: The changed voice is the interesting thing here. A familiar world rewritten with melancholy wit about the dead who came before you. The chimney's explicit carry rule and the gentle death text felt like thoughtful changes. Some of the map is altered too (Round Room cave-ins, the lake at the reservoir).

prose.why: Wherever someone has written a description, it is excellent: precise, funny, often sad, with real sentence rhythm (the troll, the bat, the chasm, the trident, the skeleton, the rusty knife). It falls short of a 5 because the old terse room text remains in many places, mirror rooms and maze rooms are word-for-word identical, and repeat visits print only the room name, so the house style is uneven.
